passage_1.text:
Cuttlefish are full of personality, as behavioral ecologist Alexandra Schnell found out while researching the cephalopod's potential to display self-control. "Self-control is thought to be the cornerstone of intelligence, as it is an important prerequisite for complex decision-making and planning for the future," says Schnell.

Schnell's study used a modified version of the "marshmallow test". During the original marshmallow test, psychologist Walter Mischel presented children between age four and six with one marshmallow. He told them that if they waited 15 minutes and didn't eat it, he would give them a second marshmallo. A long-term follow-up study showed that the children who waited for the second marshmallow had more success later in life. The cuttlefish version of the experiment looked a lot different. The researchers worked with six cuttlefish under nine months old and presented them with seafood instead of sweets. Preliminary experiments showed that cuttlefishes' favorite food is live grass shrimp, while raw prawns are so-so and Asian shore crab is nearly unacceptable. Since the researchers couldn't explain to the cuttlefish that they would need to wait for their shrimp, they trained them to recognize certain shapes that indicated when a food item would become available. The symbols were pasted on transparent drawers so that the cuttlefish could see the food that was stored inside. One drawer, labeled with a circle to mean "immediate,” held raw king prawn. Another drawer, labeled with a triangle to mean "delayed,” held live grass shrimp. During a control experiment, square labels meant "never."

"If their self-control is flexible and I hadn't just trained them to wait in any context, you would expect the cuttlefish to take the immediate reward, even if it's their second preference," says Schnell. And that's what they did. That showed the researchers that cuttlefish wouldn't reject the prawns if it was the only food available. In the experimental trials, the cuttlefish didn't jump on the prawns if the live grass shrimp were labeled with a triangle many waited for the shrimp drawer to open up. Each time the cuttlefish showed it could wait, the researchers tacked another ten seconds on to the next round of waiting before releasing the shrimp. The longest that a cuttlefish waited was 130 seconds.

Schnell says that the cuttlefish usually sat at the bottom of the tank and looked at the two food items while they waited, but sometimes, they would turn away from the king prawn "as if to distract themselves from the temptation of the immediate reward." In past studies, humans, chimpanzees, parrots and dogs also tried to distract themselves while waiting for a reward.

Not every species can use self-control, but most of the animals that can share another trait in common: long, social lives. Cuttlefish, on the other hand, are solitary creatures that don't form relationships even with mates or young. "We don't know if living in a social group is important for complex cognition unless we also show those abilities are lacking in less social species," says comparative psychologist Jennifer Vonk.

passage_2.text:
We cannot travel outside our neighbourhood without passports. We must wear the same plainclothes. We must exchange our houses every ten years. We cannot avoid labour. We all go to bed at the same time. We have religious freedom, but we cannot deny that the soul dies with the body, since 'but for the fear of punishment, they would have nothing but contempt for the laws and customs of society'. In More's time, for much of the population, given the plenty and security on offer, such restraints would not have seemed overly unreasonable. For modern readers, however, Utopia appears to rely upon relentless transparency, the repression of variety, and the curtailment of privacy. Utopia provides security: but at what price? In both its external and internal relations, indeed, it seems perilously dystopian.

Such a conclusion might be fortified by examining selectively the tradition which follows More on these points. This often portrays societies where 'it would be almost impossible for man to be depraved, or wicked'. This is achieved both through institutions and mores, which underpin the common life. The passions are regulated and inequalities of wealth and distinction are minimized. Needs, vanity, and emulation are restrained, often by prizing equality and holding riches in contempt. The desire for public power is curbed. Marriage and sexual intercourse are often controlled: in Tommaso Campanella's The City of the Sun (1623), the first great literary utopia after More's, relations are forbidden to men before the age of twenty-one and women before nineteen. Communal child-rearing is normal; for Campanella this commences at age two. Greater simplicity of life, 'living according to nature', is often a result: the desire for simplicity and purity are closely related. People become more alike in appearance, opinion, and outlook than they often have been. Unity, order, and homogeneity thus prevail at the cost of individuality and diversity. This model, as J. C. Davis demonstrates, dominated early modern utopianism. And utopian homogeneity remains a familiar theme well into the twentieth century.

Given these considerations, it is not unreasonable to take as our starting point here the hypothesis that utopia and dystopia evidently share more in common than is often supposed. Indeed, they might be twins, the progeny of the same parents. Insofar as this proves to be the case, my linkage of both here will be uncomfortably close for some readers. Yet we should not mistake this argument for the assertion that all utopias are, or tend to produce, dystopias. Those who defend this proposition will find that their association here is not nearly close enough. For we have only to acknowledge the existence of thousands of successful intentional communities in which a cooperative ethos predominates and where harmony without coercion is the rule to set aside such an assertion. Here the individual's submersion in the group is consensual (though this concept is not unproblematic). It results not in enslavement but voluntary submission to group norms. Harmony is achieved without harming others.

passage_3.text:
The sleights of hand that conflate consumption with virtue are a central theme in A Thirst for Empire, a sweeping and richly detailed history of tea by the historian Erika Rappaport. How did tea evolve from an obscure "China drink" to a universal beverage imbued with civilizing properties? The answer, in brief, revolves around this conflation, not only by profit-motivated marketers but by a wide variety of interest groups. While abundant historical records have allowed the study of how tea itself moved from east to west, Rappaport is focused on the movement of the idea of tea to suit particular purposes.

Beginning in the 1700s, the temperance movement advocated for tea as a pleasure that cheered but did not inebriate, and industrialists soon borrowed this moral argument in advancing their case for free trade in tea (and hence more open markets for their textiles). Factory owners joined in, compelled by the cause of a sober workforce, while Christian missionaries discovered that tea "would soothe any colonial encounter". During the Second World War, tea service was presented as a social and patriotic activity that uplifted soldiers and calmed refugees.

But it was tea's consumer-directed marketing by importers and retailers - and later by brands- that most closely portends current trade debates. An early version of the "farm to table” movement was sparked by anti-Chinese sentiment and concerns over trade deficits, as well as by the reality and threat of adulterated tea containing dirt and hedge clippings. Lipton was soon advertising "from the Garden to Tea Cup" supply chains originating in British India and supervised by "educated Englishmen". While tea marketing always presented direct consumer benefits (health, energy, relaxation), tea drinkers were also assured that they were participating in a larger noble project that advanced the causes of family, nation and civilization.

Rappaport's treatment of her subject is refreshingly apolitical. Indeed, it is a virtue that readers will be unable to guess her political orientation: both the miracle of markets and capitalism's dark underbelly are evident in tea's complex story, as are the complicated effects of British colonialism. Commodity histories are now themselves commodities: recent works investigate cotton, salt, cod, sugar, chocolate, paper and milk. And morality marketing is now a commodity as well, applied to food, "fair trade" apparel and eco-tourism. Yet tea is, Rappaport makes clear, a world apart an astonishing success story in which tea marketers not only succeeded in conveying a sense of moral elevation to the consumer but also arguably did advance the cause of civilisation and community.

I have been offered tea at a British garden party, a Bedouin campfire, a Turkish carpet shop and a Japanese chashitsu, to name a few settings. In each case the offering was more an idea – friendship, community, respect - than a drink, and in each case the idea then created a reality. It is not a stretch to say that tea marketers have advanced the particularly noble cause of human dialogue and friendship.

passage_4.text:
For the Maya of the Classic period, who lived in Southern Mexico and Central America between 250 and 900 CE, the category of 'persons' was not coincident with human beings, as it is for us. That is, human beings were persons but other, nonhuman entities could be persons, too. In order to explore the slippage of categories between 'humans' and 'persons', I examined a very specific category of ancient Maya images, found painted in scenes on ceramic vessels. I sought out instances in which faces (some combination of eyes, nose, and mouth) are shown on inanimate objects. Consider my iPhone, which needs to be fed with electricity every night, swaddled in a protective bumper, and enjoys communicating with other fellow phone beings. Does it have personhood (if at all) because it is connected to me, drawing this resource from me as an owner or source? For the Maya (who did have plenty of other communicating objects, if not smartphones), the answer was no. Nonhuman persons were not tethered to specific humans, and they did not derive their personhood from a connection with a human. It's a profoundly democratising way of understanding the world. Humans are not more important persons – we are just one of many kinds of persons who inhabit this world.

The Maya saw personhood as 'activated' by experiencing certain bodily needs and through participation in certain social activities. For example, among the faced objects that I examined, persons are marked by personal requirements (such as hunger, tiredness, physical closeness), and by community obligations (communication, interaction, ritual observance). In the images I examined, we see, for instance, faced objects being cradled in humans' arms; we also see them speaking to humans. These core elements of personhood are both turned inward, what the body or self of a person requires, and outward, what a community expects of the persons who are a part of it, underlining the reciprocal nature of community membership.

Personhood was a nonbinary proposition for the Maya. Entities were able to be persons while also being something else. The faced objects I looked at indicate that they continue to be functional, doing what objects do (a stone implement continues to chop, an incense burner continues to do its smoky work). Furthermore, the Maya visually depicted many objects in ways that indicated the material category to which they belonged – drawings of the stone implement show that a person-tool is still made of stone. One additional complexity: the incense burner (which would have been made of clay, and decorated with spiky appliques representing the sacred ceiba tree found in this region) is categorised as a person but also as a tree. With these Maya examples, we are challenged to discard the person/nonperson binary that constitutes our basic ontological outlook. The porousness of boundaries that we have seen in the Maya world points towards the possibility of living with a certain uncategorisability of the world.

questions.question_text: All of the following constitute a point of difference between the "original" and "modified" versions of the marshmallow test EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: the former was performed over a longer time span than the latter.

options.label: B
options.text: the former had human subjects, while the latter had cuttlefish.

options.label: C
options.text: the former used verbal communication with its subjects, while the latter had to develop a symbolic means of communication.

options.label: D
options.text: the former correlated self-control and future success, while the latter correlated self-control and survival advantages.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "That showed the researchers that cuttlefish wouldn't reject the prawns if it was the only food available."

The key insight -> this line shows the study wasn't about survival at all. The researchers were just checking if cuttlefish had flexible self-control, not studying survival benefits.

Let us trace through what the passage actually says about differences:

Original test -> children, 15 minutes, verbal instructions, tracked future success

Modified test -> cuttlefish, max 130 seconds, symbol training, studied self-control flexibility

Elimination process:

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly true difference -> 15 minutes vs max 130 seconds (about 2 minutes)

🟢 Option 2 -> obviously true difference -> children vs cuttlefish explicitly stated

🟢 Option 3 -> clearly true difference -> "told them" vs "trained them to recognize shapes"

🔴 Option 4 -> false claim -> passage never says modified test studied "survival advantages." The cuttlefish study only looked at whether they could show flexible self-control, not whether this helped them survive

The confusion students have -> they might think since the study used food, it must be about survival. But the passage shows researchers were testing cognitive flexibility, not survival benefits.

Option 4 is correct because it makes up a connection that doesn't exist in the passage.

questions.question_text: In which one of the following scenarios would the cuttlefish’s behaviour demonstrate self-control?

options.label: A
options.text: raw prawns are released while an Asian shore crab drawer labelled with a triangle is placed in front of the cuttlefish, to be opened after one minute.

options.label: B
options.text: raw prawns are released while a live grass shrimp drawer labelled with a square is placed in front of the cuttlefish

options.label: C
options.text: Asian shore crabs and raw prawns are simultaneously released while a live grass shrimp drawer labelled with a triangle is placed in front of the cuttlefish, to be opened after one minute.

options.label: D
options.text: ) live grass shrimp are released while two raw prawn drawers labelled with a circle and a triangle respectively are placed in front of the cuttlefish; the triangle labelled drawer is opened after 50 seconds

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this,we need to understand what shows self-control in cuttlefish -> they must resist taking available food now to wait for better food later.

From passage: "Live grass shrimp" are their favorite, "raw prawns are so-so" and "Asian shore crab is nearly unacceptable."

From passage: "In the experimental trials, the cuttlefish didn't jump on the prawns if the live grass shrimp were labeled with a triangle—many waited for the shrimp drawer to open up."

The key insight -> Self-control means saying no to food you can eat right now to wait for better food that comes later. Like kids waiting for a second marshmallow instead of eating the first one.

Remember: Circle = immediate, Triangle = delayed, Square = never

🔴 Option 1 -> logic-error -> Cuttlefish would naturally take prawns over crab because prawns taste better. This isn't self-control, it's just choosing the better of two bad options.

🔴 Option 2 -> impossible-scenario -> Square means "never," so the shrimp will never come. Can't show self-control if there's no delayed reward to wait for.

🟢 Option 3 is correct -> Perfect self-control test. Cuttlefish have immediate food available (prawns and crabs) but must resist both to wait for their favorite food (shrimp) that comes later with the triangle label.

🔴 Option 4 -> backwards-logic -> They already have their favorite food (shrimp) immediately available. Why would they wait for worse food (prawns)? This doesn't test self-control at all.

The confusion students have: They might think Option 1 works because there's waiting involved. But self-control only counts when you're giving up something good now for something better later, not something bad now for something worse later.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if true, would best complement the passage's findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Cuttlefish wait longer than 100 seconds for the shrimp drawer to open up.

options.label: B
options.text: Cuttlefish are equally fond of live grass shrimp and raw prawn.

options.label: C
options.text: Cuttlefish live in big groups that exhibit sociability.

options.label: D
options.text: Cuttlefish cannot distinguish between geometrical shapes.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what would add value to the passage's discoveries about cuttlefish intelligence and self-control.

The passage shows cuttlefish can control themselves and wait for better food, which is surprising because most smart animals with self-control are social, but cuttlefish live alone.

From passage: "We don't know if living in a social group is important for complex cognition unless we also show those abilities are lacking in less social species"

The key insight -> Researcher wonders if being social helps animals be smart -> Cuttlefish are smart but not social -> This creates an interesting puzzle about what makes animals intelligent.

🔴 Option 1 -> already-covered -> Passage says longest wait was 130 seconds, so waiting "longer than 100 seconds" just repeats what we already know

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts-passage -> Passage clearly states live grass shrimp is favorite food while raw prawns are just "so-so"

🟢 Option 3 -> perfect-complement -> If cuttlefish were actually social (not solitary as passage claims), this would support the theory that social life helps complex thinking

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts-experiment -> Cuttlefish were successfully trained to recognize different shapes (circle, triangle, square) in the study

From passage: "Cuttlefish, on the other hand, are solitary creatures that don't form relationships"

The beauty of Option 3 -> If cuttlefish were social instead of solitary, it would strengthen the connection between social living and intelligence -> This would complement (add support to) the research findings about smart animals being social.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following cannot be inferred from Alexandra Schnell's experiment?

options.label: A
options.text: Cuttlefish exert self-control with the help of diversions.

options.label: B
options.text: Cuttlefish exercise choice when it comes to food

options.label: C
options.text: Intelligence in a species is impossible without sociability.

options.label: D
options.text: Like human children, cuttlefish are capable of self-control.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what cannot be inferred from the experiment.

Step-by-step thought process:

The experiment tested if cuttlefish have self-control -> They used a modified marshmallow test -> Cuttlefish waited up to 130 seconds for better food -> This shows they can delay gratification

From passage: "We don't know if living in a social group is important for complex cognition unless we also show those abilities are lacking in less social species"

Key insight -> Cuttlefish are solitary but still showed intelligence/self-control -> This actually suggests intelligence is possible without being social.

Option Analysis:

🟢 Option 1 -> Can be inferred -> Passage says cuttlefish "would turn away from the king prawn as if to distract themselves" - clear evidence of using diversions

🟢 Option 2 -> Can be inferred -> Passage shows they prefer "live grass shrimp" over "raw prawns" and waited for their favorite - clear food choices

🔴 Option 3 -> Cannot be inferred -> This is backwards! The experiment shows cuttlefish (who are NOT social) still have intelligence. The researcher even says "we don't know if social groups are needed for intelligence." The evidence actually suggests intelligence can exist without sociability.

🟢 Option 4 -> Can be inferred -> The whole experiment was based on testing self-control like in human children, and cuttlefish succeeded by waiting up to 130 seconds

Student confusion: You might think Option 3 sounds logical since many smart animals are social. But the passage specifically shows cuttlefish break this pattern - they're smart but not social.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: utopian and dystopian societies are twins, the progeny of the same parents.

options.label: B
options.text: it is possible to see utopias as dystopias, with a change in perspective, because one person's utopia could be seen as another's dystopia.

options.label: C
options.text: utopian societies exist in a long tradition of literature dealing with imaginary people practicing imaginary customs, in imaginary worlds.

options.label: D
options.text: many conceptions of utopian societies emphasise the importance of social uniformity and cultural homogeneity.

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this EXCEPT question,we need to find which statement cannot be supported by the passage.

From passage: "Given these considerations, it is not unreasonable to take as our starting point here the hypothesis that utopia and dystopia evidently share more in common than is often supposed. Indeed, they might be twins, the progeny of the same parents."

The key insight here: The author uses "might be" (possibility) not "are" (certainty). This is crucial for EXCEPT questions -> look for overstatements or claims the passage doesn't fully support.

The passage shows how utopias can seem dystopian from different perspectives -> More's society seemed reasonable to his time but oppressive to modern readers -> this suggests perspective matters in judging societies.

🟠 Option 1 -> degree-error -> states as definitive fact what passage presents as possibility. Passage says utopia and dystopia "might be twins" but option claims they "are twins" - this overstates the certainty.

🟢 Option 2 -> supported -> passage shows how More's utopia seemed reasonable to his era but dystopian to modern readers, proving perspective changes interpretation.

🟢 Option 3 -> supported -> passage traces literary tradition from More (1516) to Campanella (1623) to twentieth century, showing long literary tradition of imaginary utopian worlds.

🟢 Option 4 -> supported -> passage explicitly states "Unity, order, and homogeneity thus prevail" and "utopian homogeneity remains a familiar theme" - directly confirms emphasis on uniformity.

The confusion students face: Options 2, 3, and 4 all have clear textual support. Option 1 sounds like it's supported because the passage discusses the relationship between utopia and dystopia, but it crosses the line from "might be" to "are" - making an absolute claim the passage doesn't make.

questions.question_text: Which sequence of words below best captures the narrative of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Relentless transparency – Homogeneity – Utopia – Dystopia.

options.label: B
options.text: Curtailment of privacy – Dystopia – Utopia – Intentional community.

options.label: C
options.text: Utopia – Security – Dystopia – Coercion.

options.label: D
options.text: Utopia – Security – Homogeneity – Intentional community.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage starts with More's Utopia -> then discusses what it offers (security) -> then shows what results from utopian controls (homogeneity) -> finally ends discussing successful intentional communities.

From passage: "Utopia provides security: but at what price?" and later "Unity, order, and homogeneity thus prevail at the cost of individuality and diversity" and finally "thousands of successful intentional communities"

Thought process: Start with Utopia concept -> leads to security benefits -> results in homogeneity problem -> ends with intentional community examples.

🔴 Option 1 -> sequence-error -> starts with "relentless transparency" (a detail) instead of the main concept "Utopia" that begins the whole discussion

🔴 Option 2 -> sequence-error -> puts "Dystopia" before "Utopia" but passage discusses utopia first, then its dystopian aspects

🟠 Option 3 -> ending-error -> captures first part correctly (Utopia-Security-Dystopia) but ends with "coercion" instead of the passage's final focus on successful "intentional communities"

🟢 Option 4 -> perfect-sequence -> follows exact narrative flow: introduces Utopia -> discusses security it provides -> shows homogeneity result -> ends with intentional communities discussion

The key insight: follow the chronological narrative, not just random important words from the passage. Option 4 captures this perfectly.

questions.question_text: All of the following arguments are made in the passage EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: in More’s time, there was plenty and security, so people did not need restraints that could appear unreasonable

options.label: B
options.text: in early modern utopianism, the stability of utopian societies was seen to be achieved only with individuals surrendering their sense of self

options.label: C
options.text: there have been thousands of communities where homogeneity and stability have been achieved through choice, rather than by force.

options.label: D
options.text: the tradition of utopian literature has often shown societies in which it would be nearly impossible for anyone to be sinful or criminal.

questions.explanation_text:
The key is understanding what the passage actually says about More's time and restraints.

From passage: "In More's time, for much of the population, given the plenty and security on offer, such restraints would not have seemed overly unreasonable."

This means: plenty and security made restraints seem reasonable -> people still had restraints, they just didn't mind them because of the benefits.

🔴 Option 1 -> misinterprets the passage -> says people "did not need restraints" but passage shows restraints existed and were just tolerable because of benefits

The passage never argues people didn't need restraints. It says the opposite - restraints existed but seemed reasonable because of plenty/security.

🟢 Option 2 -> supported by passage -> "Unity, order, and homogeneity thus prevail at the cost of individuality and diversity. This model...dominated early modern utopianism"

🟢 Option 3 -> supported by passage -> "thousands of successful intentional communities...where harmony without coercion is the rule...consensual...voluntary submission"

🟢 Option 4 -> supported by passage -> "This often portrays societies where 'it would be almost impossible for man to be depraved, or wicked'"

Elimination strategy: In EXCEPT questions, look for the option that twists or misrepresents what the passage actually says. Options 2, 3, and 4 all have direct support in the text. Option 1 completely misreads the passage - it suggests restraints weren't needed, when the passage shows restraints definitely existed but were just acceptable because of the benefits offered.

questions.question_text: Following from the passage, which one of the following may be seen as a characteristic of a utopian society?

options.label: A
options.text: The regulation of homogeneity through promoting competitive heterogeneity.

options.label: B
options.text: A society where public power is earned through merit rather than through privilege.

options.label: C
options.text: A society without any laws to restrain one's individuality.

options.label: D
options.text: Institutional surveillance of every individual to ensure his/her security and welfare

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the key evidence about how utopian societies work.

The passage shows utopias trade freedom for security -> strict controls everywhere -> surveillance to maintain order -> this ensures people's basic needs and safety.

From passage: "Utopia appears to rely upon relentless transparency, the repression of variety, and the curtailment of privacy. Utopia provides security: but at what price?"

The thought process: Utopias promise safety and basic needs -> but they control everything to deliver this -> they watch everyone constantly -> this surveillance is justified as protecting people's welfare.

Students often get confused between what utopias should do versus what they actually do in practice. The passage focuses on the reality of how utopias function.

🔴 Option 1 -> contradictory -> says "promoting competitive heterogeneity" but passage clearly states utopias create "homogeneity" and sameness, not variety or competition

🟠 Option 2 -> scope-error -> passage mentions curbing "desire for public power" but doesn't discuss merit vs privilege systems for earning power

🔴 Option 3 -> opposite-truth -> claims "no laws to restrain individuality" but passage lists tons of restrictions like same clothes, controlled travel, forced labor, regulated bedtimes

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> matches "relentless transparency" + all the controls mentioned + the trade-off where utopias "provide security" through watching and controlling everyone's behavior

From passage: "given the plenty and security on offer, such restraints would not have seemed overly unreasonable"

The key insight: Utopias justify constant surveillance and control by claiming it's for people's own good - their security and welfare.

questions.question_text: According to this book review, A Thirst for Empire says that, in addition to "profit-motivated marketers", tea drinking was promoted in Britain by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the anti-alcohol lobby as a substitute for the consumption of liquor.

options.label: B
options.text: tea drinkers lobbying for product diversity.

options.label: C
options.text: manufacturers who were pressing for duty-free imports

options.label: D
options.text: factories to instill sobriety in their labour

questions.explanation_text:
The passage clearly lists several groups that promoted tea ->we need to match each option to find the one that's missing.

From passage: "Beginning in the 1700s, the temperance movement advocated for tea as a pleasure that cheered but did not inebriate, and industrialists soon borrowed this moral argument in advancing their case for free trade in tea... Factory owners joined in, compelled by the cause of a sober workforce"

My thought process: Scan paragraph 2 for groups mentioned -> Match each option -> Find the odd one out -> The one not mentioned = correct answer

🟢 Option 1 -> mentioned -> temperance movement = anti-alcohol lobby promoting tea instead of liquor

🔴 Option 2 -> not mentioned -> passage never says tea drinkers themselves lobbied for product diversity

🟢 Option 3 -> mentioned -> industrialists wanted free trade in tea (duty-free imports)

🟢 Option 4 -> mentioned -> factory owners wanted sober workforce through tea

The confusion here: Students might think all groups sound reasonable, but remember -> this is an EXCEPT question.we need to find what's NOT in the passage, not what makes sense logically.

Option 2 talks about tea drinkers lobbying for variety, but the passage only mentions groups promoting tea consumption in general, not consumers asking for more product options.

questions.question_text: This book review argues that, according to Rappaport, tea is unlike other "morality" products because it:

options.label: A
options.text: was marketed by a wide range of interest groups.

options.label: B
options.text: was actively encouraged by interest groups in the government

options.label: C
options.text: appealed to a universal group and not just to a niche section of people

options.label: D
options.text: had an actual beneficial effect on social interaction and society in general

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this question,we need to find what makes tea different from other "morality" products according to the author.

From passage: "Commodity histories are now themselves commodities... And morality marketing is now a commodity as well, applied to food, 'fair trade' apparel and eco-tourism. Yet tea is, Rappaport makes clear, a world apart an astonishing success story in which tea marketers not only succeeded in conveying a sense of moral elevation to the consumer but also arguably did advance the cause of civilisation and community."

The key phrase is "tea is... a world apart" -> This tells me tea is different from other morality products -> The difference is that tea marketers didn't just market morality, they "arguably did advance the cause of civilisation and community" -> So tea actually had real beneficial effects.

The final paragraph confirms this with real examples -> Tea created actual friendship and dialogue -> "It is not a stretch to say that tea marketers have advanced the particularly noble cause of human dialogue and friendship."

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Yes, many groups marketed tea, but this doesn't explain why tea is different from other morality products. Many products have wide marketing.

🔴 Option 2 -> scope-error -> The passage mentions various groups but doesn't focus on government encouragement as the distinguishing factor. Too narrow.

🟠 Option 3 -> context-shift -> The passage doesn't compare tea's appeal to different groups. It compares tea's actual effects vs. just marketing claims.

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> Captures the main point perfectly. Unlike other "morality" products that just use marketing claims, tea actually "did advance the cause of civilisation and community" and created real "human dialogue and friendship."

questions.question_text: The author of this book review is LEAST likely to support the view that:

options.label: A
options.text: tea drinking has become a social ritual worldwide

options.label: B
options.text: the ritual of drinking tea promotes congeniality and camaraderie

options.label: C
options.text: tea drinking was sometimes promoted as a patriotic duty

options.label: D
options.text: tea became the leading drink in Britain in the nineteenth century

questions.explanation_text:
The question asks what the author would be LEAST likely to support. This means we need to find the option that either contradicts the passage or isn't supported by any evidence in the text.

Step 1: Look for direct evidence

The passage gives us clear examples of the author's views. When the author shares personal experiences and makes conclusions, those show what they support.

Step 2: Check each option against the text

We need to see which options have clear support in the passage and which one doesn't.

From passage: "I have been offered tea at a British garden party, a Bedouin campfire, a Turkish carpet shop and a Japanese chashitsu... In each case the offering was more an idea – friendship, community, respect - than a drink"

This shows the author believes tea creates social connections worldwide -> supports options about social rituals and friendship.

From passage: "During the Second World War, tea service was presented as a social and patriotic activity that uplifted soldiers and calmed refugees"

This directly supports the idea that tea was promoted for patriotic reasons.

🟢 Option 1 -> supported -> Author gives examples from British, Bedouin, Turkish, and Japanese settings, showing tea as a worldwide social ritual

🟢 Option 2 -> supported -> Author says tea offerings create "friendship, community, respect" and promote "human dialogue and friendship"

🟢 Option 3 -> supported -> Passage directly states tea was "presented as a social and patriotic activity" during WWII

🔴 Option 4 -> no evidence -> Passage never mentions tea becoming the "leading drink" in Britain during the 19th century. Author discusses tea's evolution but doesn't make this specific claim about Britain or ranking it as #1 drink.

The author would be LEAST likely to support Option 4 because there's simply no evidence for this claim in the passage.

questions.question_text: Today, “conflating consumption with virtue” can be seen in the marketing of:

options.label: A
options.text: ergonomically designed products

options.label: B
options.text: sustainably farmed foods

options.label: C
options.text: travel to pristine destinations

options.label: D
options.text: natural health supplements.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage gives us specific examples in the second-to-last paragraph where it talks about current marketing practices.

From passage: "And morality marketing is now a commodity as well, applied to food, 'fair trade' apparel and eco-tourism."

The passage directly tells us that moral marketing (making consumption seem virtuous) is now applied to three areas: food, fair trade apparel, and eco-tourism.

Sowe need to find which option matches one of these three categories -> food is the most obvious match.

Option Analysis:

🔴 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> ergonomically designed products aren't mentioned in the passage and ergonomics is about comfort, not moral virtue

🟢 Option 2 -> correct match -> "sustainably farmed foods" directly matches the "food" category mentioned in the passage, and sustainability is clearly a virtue being marketed to consumers

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> "travel to pristine destinations" is close to "eco-tourism" but doesn't capture the moral/environmental virtue aspect that makes eco-tourism special

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> natural health supplements aren't mentioned in the passage's list of current morality marketing examples

The key insight: sustainably farmed foods perfectly fits the passage's mention of how moral marketing is applied to food -> sustainability = virtue, farming = food production.

questions.question_text: On the basis of the passage, which one of the following worldviews can be inferred to be closest to that of the Classic Maya?

options.label: A
options.text: A futuristic society that perceives robots to be persons as well as robots because of their similarity to humans.

options.label: B
options.text: A tribe that perceives plants as person-plants because they form an ecosystem and are marked by needs of nutrition.

options.label: C
options.text: A tribe that perceives its hunting weapons as sacred person-arte facts because of their significance to its survival.

options.label: D
options.text: A tribe that perceives its utensils as person-utensils in light of their functionality and bodily needs.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which worldview matches the Maya's way of seeing personhood. From passage: "Nonhuman persons were not tethered to specific humans, and they did not derive their personhood from a connection with a human."

The key insight -> Maya personhood was independent from humans. Objects/beings were persons because of their own needs and community roles, not because humans found them useful.

From passage: "Maya saw personhood as 'activated' by experiencing certain bodily needs and through participation in certain social activities."

Process -> Maya personhood came from: internal needs (hunger, tiredness) + community participation (communication, ritual) -> NOT from human connection.

Nowwe need to eliminate options that make personhood depend on humans:

🔴 Option 1 -> human-centered -> robots are persons because they're similar to humans - this makes humans the standard, opposite of Maya democratizing view

🔴 Option 3 -> human-utility focused -> weapons are persons because of their significance to human survival - personhood comes from serving humans, not independent existence

🔴 Option 4 -> function-based -> utensils are persons based on their functionality - this suggests usefulness to humans rather than independent personhood

🟢 Option 2 is correct -> plants have personhood because of their own nutritional needs and role in ecosystem (community) - matches Maya view of independent personhood based on internal needs + community participation

The confusion might be between Options 2 and 4 since both mention needs. But Option 4's "functionality" suggests human use, while Option 2 focuses purely on the plants' own needs and ecosystem role - no human connection required.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if true, would not undermine the democratising potential of the Classic Maya worldview?

options.label: A
options.text: They understood the stone implement and the incense burner in a purely human form.

options.label: B
options.text: They believed that animals like cats and dogs that live in proximity to humans have a more clearly articulated personhood

options.label: C
options.text: They depicted their human healers with physical attributes of local medicinal plants.

options.label: D
options.text: While they believed in the personhood of objects and plants, they did not believe in the personhood of rivers and animals.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Humans are not more important persons – we are just one of many kinds of persons who inhabit this world."

The Maya worldview is democratising because -> it doesn't put humans above other beings -> nonhuman entities can be persons too -> personhood isn't tied to human connection -> creates equality between different types of persons.

🔴 Option 1 -> contradicts core concept -> says objects were understood in "purely human form" but passage shows objects kept their material nature while being persons (stone tool still made of stone)

🔴 Option 2 -> human-dependency error -> suggests animals near humans have "more clearly articulated personhood" but passage explicitly states nonhuman persons were "not tethered to specific humans" and didn't derive personhood from human connection

🟢 Option 3 -> supports democratising view -> shows humans taking on plant attributes, which demonstrates equality and interconnection rather than human superiority -> aligns perfectly with "many kinds of persons" concept

🔴 Option 4 -> creates arbitrary boundaries -> limits personhood to only objects and plants while excluding rivers and animals -> contradicts the inclusive "many kinds of persons" principle

From passage: "Personhood was a nonbinary proposition for the Maya. Entities were able to be persons while also being something else."

Option 3 shows this perfectly -> human healers could have plant attributes -> demonstrates the boundary-crossing that made the Maya worldview democratising -> doesn't undermine it at all.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best explains the "additional complexity" that the example of the incense burner illustrates regarding personhood for the Classic Maya?

options.label: A
options.text: The example complicates the nonbinary understanding of personhood by bringing in the sacred, establishing the porosity of the divine and the profane.

options.label: B
options.text: The example adds a new layer to the nonbinary understanding of personhood by bringing in a third category that shares a similar relation with the previous two.

options.label: C
options.text: The example provides an exception to the nonbinary understanding of person hood that the passage had hitherto established.

options.label: D
options.text: The example adds a new layer to the nonbinary understanding of personhood by bringing in a third category that shares a dissimilar relation with the previous two.

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this question,we need to find what "additional complexity" the incense burner example shows about Maya personhood.

Step 1: Find the "additional complexity" in the passage

Step 2: Understand how it relates to Maya nonbinary personhood concept

Step 3: Match this understanding with the right option

From passage: "One additional complexity: the incense burner (which would have been made of clay, and decorated with spiky appliques representing the sacred ceiba tree found in this region) is categorised as a person but also as a tree."

The passage already explained that Maya objects can be both persons and functional objects (like stone tools). The incense burner adds another layer -> it's a person and an object and a tree. So we go from two categories to three categories.

The key insight -> Maya personhood breaks our simple "person vs nonperson" thinking. The incense burner shows this even more clearly by belonging to three categories at once.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses on sacred vs profane, but passage isn't about religious categories. It's about how many different things one entity can be at the same time.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures it perfectly. Takes the existing two categories (person + object) and adds a third (tree). All three relate to the incense burner in the same way - it literally IS all three things.

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> calls it an "exception" but passage presents it as another example that supports the nonbinary idea, not something that goes against it.

🔴 Option 4 -> degree-error -> right about third category but wrong about "dissimilar relation." The incense burner relates to all three categories the same way - by being all three things.

From passage: "With these Maya examples, we are challenged to discard the person/nonperson binary that constitutes our basic ontological outlook."

The incense burner shows we need to think beyond just two categories -> it adds tree as a third category that works just like the other two.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if true about the Classic Maya, would invalidate the purpose of the iPhone example in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The clay incense burner with spiky appliques was categorised only as a person and not as a tree by the Classic Maya.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike modern societies equipped with mobile phones, the Classic Maya did not have any communicating objects

options.label: C
options.text: The personhood of the incense burner and the stone chopper was a function of their usefulness to humans.

options.label: D
options.text: Classic Maya songs represent both humans and non-living objects as characters, talking and interacting with each other.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Consider my iPhone, which needs to be fed with electricity every night... Does it have personhood (if at all) because it is connected to me, drawing this resource from me as an owner or source? For the Maya... the answer was no."

The iPhone example's whole purpose is to show the difference between us and the Maya -> We might think objects get personhood from being connected to humans, but Maya said NO.

If Maya objects actually DID get personhood from being useful to humans, then the iPhone example becomes meaningless -> both iPhone and Maya objects would get personhood the same way (from human connection).

🔴 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> talks about tree vs person categories, but iPhone example is about human connection, not categories

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts passage -> passage clearly says Maya "did have plenty of other communicating objects"

🟢 Option 3 -> directly invalidates -> if Maya personhood came from usefulness to humans, then iPhone example fails because both iPhone and Maya objects would get personhood from human connection

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> songs showing interactions doesn't touch the core issue of where personhood comes from

The key insight: iPhone example works only because Maya personhood was independent of human usefulness. If it wasn't independent, the comparison falls apart.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. The legal status of resources mined in space remains ambiguous; and while the market for asteroid minerals is currently nonexistent, this is likely to change as technical hurdles diminish.
  2. Outer space is a commons, and all of it is open for exploration, however, space law developed in the 1950s and 60s is state-centric and arguably ill-suited to a commercial future.
  3. Laws adopted by the US and Luxembourg are first steps, but they only protect firms from competing claims by their compatriots; a Chinese company will not be bound by US law.
  4. Critics say the US is conferring rights that it has no authority to confer; Russia in particular has condemned this, citing the US' disrespect for international law.
  5. At issue now is commercial activity, as private firms rather than nation states look to space for profit.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "At issue now is commercial activity, as private firms rather than nation states look to space for profit" and "The legal status of resources mined in space remains ambiguous"

The main topic is clearly about space mining rights and how laws are changing from old government-focused rules to new commercial needs.

Let us trace the logical flow: Commercial space activity is growing -> Legal status is unclear -> Old laws don't work for business -> New laws have limits

🟢 Sentences 1, 2, 3, 5 form a coherent paragraph:

  • Sentence 5: Sets up the issue (commercial space activity)
  • Sentence 1: Explains the legal problem (ambiguous rights)
  • Sentence 2: Why old laws don't work (state-centric, not commercial)
  • Sentence 3: Problems with new laws (only protect same-country companies)

🔴 Sentence 4 is the odd one out: It talks about general criticism of US international law behavior, but doesn't specifically connect to space mining or asteroid resources. While it mentions "rights," it could be about any international issue, not necessarily space.

The other sentences use specific space terms like "asteroid minerals," "mined in space," and "space for profit." Sentence 4 is too vague and general about international law disputes.

Answer: 4

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. The work is more than the text, for the text only takes on life, when it is realized and furthermore the realization is by no means independent of the individual disposition of the reader.
  2. The convergence of text and reader brings the literary work into existence and this convergence is not to be identified either with the reality of the text or with the individual disposition of the reader.
  3. From this polarity it follows that the literary work cannot be completely identical with the text, or with the realization of the text, but in fact must lie halfway between the two.
  4. The literary work has two poles, which we might call the artistic and the aesthetic; the artistic refers to the text created by the author, and the aesthetic to the realization accomplished by the reader.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the introduction sentence -> Look for a sentence that introduces a new concept without referring to something already mentioned.

From passage: "The literary work has two poles, which we might call the artistic and the aesthetic"

Sentence 4 introduces the key concept of "two poles" without assuming prior knowledge -> This is your starting point.

Step 2: Look for connecting words that link sentences together:

  • Sentence 3 starts with "From this polarity" -> refers back to the "two poles" in sentence 4
  • Sentence 1 uses "furthermore" -> continues an existing discussion
  • Sentence 2 mentions "convergence" -> seems like a conclusion

Logical chain: 4 (introduces poles) -> 3 (refers to "this polarity") -> 1 (elaborates with "furthermore") -> 2 (concludes with "convergence")

Step 3: Check the flow makes sense:

4 -> Sets up artistic pole (text) vs aesthetic pole (reader)

3 -> Says work lies "halfway between the two" poles

1 -> Explains why it's more than just text (needs reader realization)

2 -> Concludes how text + reader = literary work

From passage: "The convergence of text and reader brings the literary work into existence"

This wraps up the argument perfectly -> Sentence 2 is the natural conclusion.

Answer: 4312

The key is finding the sentence that doesn't depend on others (sentence 4), then following the logical connections step by step.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

McGurk and MacDonald (1976) reported a powerful multisensory illusion occurring with audio-visual speech. They recorded a voice articulating a consonant 'ba-ba-ba' and dubbed it with a face articulating another consonant 'ga-ga-ga'. Even though the acoustic speech signal was well recognized alone, it was heard as another consonant after dubbing with incongruent visual speech i.e., 'da-da-da'. The illusion, termed as the McGurk effect, has been replicated many times, and it has sparked an abundance of research. The reason for the great impact is that this is a striking demonstration of multisensory integration, where that auditory and visual information is merged into a unified, integrated percept.

options.label: A
options.text: When the auditory speech signal does not match the visual speech movements, the acoustic speech signal is confusing and integration of the two is imperfect.

options.label: B
options.text: The McGurk effect which is a demonstration of multisensory integration has been replicated many times.

options.label: C
options.text: When the quality of auditory information is poor, the visual information wins over the auditory information.

options.label: D
options.text: Visual speech mismatched with auditory speech can result in the perception of an entirely different message: this illusion is known as the McGurk effect.

questions.explanation_text:
The key to solving this question is understanding what the McGurk effect actually demonstrates. From passage: "They recorded a voice articulating a consonant 'ba-ba-ba' and dubbed it with a face articulating another consonant 'ga-ga-ga'... it was heard as another consonant after dubbing with incongruent visual speech i.e., 'da-da-da'."

The passage shows a clear process: audio 'ba' + visual 'ga' = perceived 'da'. This isn't confusion or poor integration -> it's the brain creating something completely new from two different inputs.

When choosing between options, students often get confused between Options 1 and 4. 🔴 Option 1 -> degree-error -> calls integration "imperfect" and "confusing" but the passage shows integration works perfectly to create a clear, unified sound ('da-da-da'). The brain isn't confused - it's doing exactly what it's designed to do.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions replication correctly but completely ignores the main finding about what the McGurk effect actually is. It's like describing a movie by only saying "it was popular."

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> talks about "poor quality" audio, but passage clearly states the acoustic signal "was well recognized alone." Also suggests one sense "wins over" another, but the effect creates something entirely different from both inputs.

🟢 Option 4 -> captures both the core mechanism (mismatch creates different perception) and correctly identifies this as the McGurk effect. It matches the passage's key finding perfectly.

The elimination process: Look for what actually happens in the experiment -> 'ba' + 'ga' = 'da' (entirely different message). Only Option 4 captures this essence.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Developing countries are becoming hotbeds of business innovation in much the same way as Japan did from the 1950s onwards. They are reinventing systems of production and distribution, and experimenting with entirely new business models. Why are countries that were until recently associated with cheap hands now becoming leaders in innovation? Driven by a mixture of ambition and fear they are relentlessly climbing up the value chain. Emerging-market champions have not only proved highly competitive in their own backyards, they are also going global themselves.

options.label: A
options.text: Innovations in production and distribution are helping emerging economies compete with countries to which they once supplied cheap labour.

options.label: B
options.text: Competition has driven emerging economies, once suppliers of cheap labour, to become innovators of business models that have enabled them to move up the value chain and goglobal.

options.label: C
options.text: Developing countries are being forced to invent new business models which challenge the old business models, so they can remain competitive domestically.

options.label: D
options.text: Production and distribution models are going through rapid innovations worldwide as developed countries are being challenged by their earlier suppliers from the developing world.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "They are reinventing systems of production and distribution, and experimenting with entirely new business models... Driven by a mixture of ambition and fear they are relentlessly climbing up the value chain."

The passage shows a clear journey: cheap labor -> business innovation -> moving up value chain -> going global. The key insight is they're innovating in THREE areas: production, distribution, AND business models.

Elimination Strategy: Look for options that miss key elements or change the scope/tone of the passage.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> mentions production and distribution correctly but completely ignores business models (which the passage emphasizes). Also says "compete with countries they supplied to" rather than "going global themselves."

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures the complete journey from cheap labor suppliers to business model innovators, mentions moving up value chain and going global. Gets the essence right.

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> says "being forced" when passage says "driven by ambition and fear." Also says "remain competitive domestically" when passage clearly states they're "going global." Wrong tone and scope.

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> focuses only on production and distribution, completely misses business models. Also makes it sound like a worldwide trend rather than specifically about developing countries' transformation.

The confusion here might be between Options 1 and 2. Option 1 sounds good because it mentions production/distribution, but it misses the crucial "business models" part. Option 2 captures the complete transformation story that the passage tells.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. There is a dark side to academic research, especially in India, and at its centre is the phenomenon of predatory journals.
  2. But in truth, as long as you pay, you can get anything published.
  3. In look and feel thus, they are exactly like any reputed journal.
  4. They claim to be indexed in the most influential databases, say they possess editorial boards that comprise top scientists and researchers, and claim to have a rigorous peer-review structure.
  5. But a large section of researchers and scientists across the world are at the receiving end of nothing short of an academic publishing scam.
questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which sentence doesn't fit with the other four to form a coherent paragraph. From passage: "There is a dark side to academic research, especially in India, and at its centre is the phenomenon of predatory journals."

The key here is scope consistency. Sentence 1 sets up the topic -> predatory journals specifically in India. Nowwe need to see which sentences follow this India-focused discussion.

Logical flow process:

  • Sentence 1 -> introduces problem (predatory journals in India)
  • Sentence 4 -> describes what these journals claim to be
  • Sentence 3 -> explains how they look legitimate
  • Sentence 2 -> reveals the harsh reality (pay to publish)

This creates a perfect flow: problem introduction -> false claims -> fake appearance -> ugly truth

The elimination process:

🟢 Sentences 1, 2, 3, 4 -> All stay focused on the India-specific context and flow logically from introduction to revelation

🔴 Sentence 5 -> scope-error -> shifts from "especially in India" to "across the world" - this breaks the geographical focus and doesn't connect smoothly with the India-specific discussion

The passage maintains tight focus on India's predatory journal problem, but sentence 5 suddenly jumps to a global perspective without any transition, making it the odd one out.

Answer: 5

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. In the central nervous systems of other animal species, such a comprehensive regeneration of neurons has not yet been proven beyond doubt.
  2. Biologists from the University of Bayreuth have discovered a uniquely rapid form of regeneration in injured neurons and their function in the central nervous system of zebrafish.
  3. They studied the Mauthner cells, which are solely responsible for the escape behaviour of the fish, and previously regarded as incapable of regeneration.
  4. However, their ability to regenerate crucially depends on the location of the injury.
questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step thought process:

First, we look for the opening sentence - one that introduces a new topic without depending on previous information.

Sentence 2 is a complete introduction: "Biologists from the University of Bayreuth have discovered..." This doesn't need any prior context.

Next, we follow the pronoun connections -> Sentence 3 starts with "They studied" -> This "They" clearly refers to the "Biologists" mentioned in sentence 2.

Then we look for transition words -> Sentence 4 starts with "However" -> This word shows it's adding a limitation to what came before.

Finally, sentence 1 provides a broader comparison -> It contrasts the zebrafish discovery with other animal species.

Logical flow: Introduction -> Specific study details -> Limitation -> Broader context

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. A popular response is the exhortation to plant more trees.
  2. It seems all but certain that global warming will go well above two degrees—quite how high no one knows yet.
  3. Burning them releases it, which is why the scale of forest fires in the Amazon basin last year garnered headlines.
  4. This is because trees sequester carbon by absorbing carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: The sentences discuss global warming, tree planting as a solution, and the science behind it.

First, identify what each sentence does:

  • Sentence 2: States a problem (global warming)
  • Sentence 1: Gives a solution (plant trees)
  • Sentence 4: Explains why the solution works (trees absorb carbon)
  • Sentence 3: Shows the opposite effect (burning releases carbon)

Thought process: Problem -> Solution -> Why solution works -> Why opposite is bad

The key connector is "it" in sentence 3, which must refer to "carbon" from sentence 4. This means sentence 4 must come before sentence 3.

Step-by-step elimination:

Look for the starting sentence -> Sentence 2 introduces the main problem (global warming), so it should start the paragraph.

Find the logical sequence -> After stating the problem, we need the response (sentence 1), then explanation (sentence 4), then the contrasting example (sentence 3).

Check pronoun references -> "This" in sentence 4 refers to tree planting from sentence 1. "It" in sentence 3 refers to carbon from sentence 4.

The flow: Global warming concern (2) -> Popular solution (1) -> Scientific explanation (4) -> Contrasting example showing why fires are bad (3)

Answer: 2143

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Foreign peacekeepers often exist in a bubble in the poor countries in which they are deployed; they live in posh compounds, drive fancy vehicles, and distance themselves from locals. This may be partially justified as they are outsiders, living in constant fear, performing a job that is emotionally draining. But they are often despised by the locals, and many would like them to leave. A better solution would be bottom-up peace building, which would involve their spending more time working with communities, understanding their grievances and earning their trust, rather than only meeting government officials.

options.label: A
options.text: The environment in poor countries has tended to make foreign peacekeeping forces live in enclaves, but it is time to change this scenario.

options.label: B
options.text: Extravagant lifestyles and an aloof attitude among the foreigners working as peacekeepers in poor countries have justifiably make them the target of local anger.

options.label: C
options.text: Peacekeeping duties would be more effectively performed by local residents given their better understanding, knowledge and rapport with their own communities.

options.label: D
options.text: Peacekeeping forces in foreign countries have tended to be aloof for valid reasons but would be more effective if they worked more closely with local communities.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main message about foreign peacekeepers and what should change.

From passage: "Foreign peacekeepers often exist in a bubble... But they are often despised by the locals, and many would like them to leave. A better solution would be bottom-up peace building, which would involve their spending more time working with communities"

The passage structure: Problem (isolation) -> Partial justification (valid reasons) -> Consequence (local resentment) -> Solution (work with communities, not just officials)

Key insight: The passage acknowledges peacekeepers have valid reasons for isolation but argues they need to change approach -> work with locals, not replace them entirely.

Students often get confused between options that sound reasonable but miss the core message.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> blames "environment" instead of peacekeepers' choices. Misses that peacekeepers need to actively engage communities, not just change because environment forces it.

🟠 Option 2 -> degree-error -> says local anger is "justifiable" but passage says peacekeepers' isolation is "partially justified." Gets the relationship backwards - focuses on anger being right vs. peacekeepers needing to change approach.

🟠 Option 3 -> context-shift -> suggests replacing foreign peacekeepers with locals entirely. But passage wants foreign peacekeepers to work with communities -> "their spending more time working with communities" (their = peacekeepers).

🟢 Option 4 -> captures essence accurately -> acknowledges peacekeepers are aloof for valid reasons (matches "partially justified") but implies need for change (matches bottom-up solution focus).

Quick elimination tip: Look for options that either blame wrong party (Option 1), reverse the logic (Option 2), or suggest extreme solutions not mentioned (Option 3).
